--- title: "Chapter 9 – Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks" jupyter: python3 --- ## 9.1 From Biological to Artificial Neurons ### Overview Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are computational models inspired by the organization of biological neurons. Although modern neural networks are far simpler than the human brain, they follow the same fundamental principle: many simple processing units collaborate to solve complex tasks. A biological neuron receives signals through its dendrites, processes this information inside the cell body, and transmits an electrical signal through its axon when the accumulated input exceeds a certain threshold. Artificial neurons mimic this behavior mathematically. Each neuron receives several numerical inputs, assigns an importance (weight) to each one, computes their weighted sum, adds a bias term, and finally applies an activation function to determine its output. Individually, a neuron performs only a simple computation. However, when thousands or even millions of neurons are connected into multiple layers, they become capable of learning highly complex patterns directly from data. This idea forms the foundation of modern Deep Learning. --- ### Biological vs. Artificial Neuron | Biological Neuron | Artificial Neuron | |-------------------|------------------| | Dendrites receive signals | Input features | | Synapses determine signal strength | Weights | | Cell body integrates signals | Weighted sum | | Activation threshold | Activation function | | Axon transmits output | Model output | --- ### A Single Artificial Neuron A single artificial neuron performs three basic steps: 1. Receive the input features. 2. Compute a weighted sum plus a bias. 3. Apply an activation function. Mathematically, $$ z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b $$ where - $x_i$ are the input features, - $w_i$ are the weights, - $b$ is the bias. The neuron output is then $$ \hat{y}=f(z) $$ where $f(\\cdot)$ is the activation function. --- ### Interactive Example: Exploring a Single Artificial Neuron A single artificial neuron first computes $$ z = wx + b $$ and then applies an activation function: $$ \hat{y} = f(z) $$ Use the controls to explore how the parameters affect the neuron output. ::: {#cell-interactive-single-neuron .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 400) def activation(z, name): if name == "Linear": return z elif name == "ReLU": return np.maximum(0, z) elif name == "Sigmoid": return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) elif name == "Tanh": return np.tanh(z) weights = [-2, -1, 0.5, 1, 2] biases = [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2] activations = ["Linear", "ReLU", "Sigmoid", "Tanh"] fig = go.Figure() # Initial configuration initial_weight = 1 initial_bias = 0 initial_activation = "ReLU" z = initial_weight * x + initial_bias y = activation(z, initial_activation) fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=x, y=z, mode="lines", name="Linear combination", line=dict(dash="dash") ) ) fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name="Neuron output" ) ) # Precompute all possible curves configurations = [] for weight in weights: for bias in biases: for activation_name in activations: z_values = weight * x + bias output_values = activation(z_values, activation_name) configurations.append({ "weight": weight, "bias": bias, "activation": activation_name, "z": z_values, "output": output_values }) buttons = [] for config in configurations: label = ( f"w={config['weight']}, " f"b={config['bias']}, " f"{config['activation']}" ) buttons.append( dict( label=label, method="update", args=[ { "y": [ config["z"], config["output"] ] }, { "title": ( "Single Artificial Neuron: " f"w={config['weight']}, " f"b={config['bias']}, " f"activation={config['activation']}" ) } ] ) ) fig.update_layout( title="Single Artificial Neuron", xaxis_title="Input x", yaxis_title="Output", yaxis=dict(range=[-8, 8]), hovermode="x unified", updatemenus=[ dict( buttons=buttons, direction="down", showactive=True, x=0, y=1.18, xanchor="left", yanchor="top" ) ], margin=dict(t=130) ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#interactive-single-neuron .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Try several configurations and observe: 1. What happens when the weight changes sign? 2. How does the bias shift the linear combination? 3. Which activation functions constrain the output? 4. Why does ReLU produce a flat region? --- ### Key Takeaways - Artificial neurons are simplified mathematical models inspired by biological neurons. - Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs. - The activation function determines the final output. - A single neuron is a simple model, but many interconnected neurons can learn highly complex relationships.
